                      *vllm.platforms.interface.set_assigned_physical_gpu_ids*
`set_assigned_physical_gpu_ids(ids)`

Set the physical GPU IDs assigned to this worker process. Called during
worker init so that device_id_to_physical_device_id() can map local_rank to
the correct physical device without relying on CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.

Idempotent: a second call with the same value is a no-op. Raises
RuntimeError if called again with a different value.

This is expected to run during single-threaded worker initialization.

                                     *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface*

Contract for `vllm.endpoint_plugins` entry points.

An endpoint plugin adds HTTP routes to the OpenAI compatible API server. Its
scope is HTTP surface only. It registers routes and optionally per app state
used by those routes. It must not open new paths into the engine by reaching
the engine the same way an in-tree serving handler does via `EngineClient`
(e.g. `engine_client.collective_rpc(...)`).

If a plugin also needs engine side behavior (a new worker side RPC method, a
custom stat, etc.) pair this entry point with one registered under
`vllm.general_plugins` (see `vllm/plugins/__init__.py`). The
`general_plugins` entry installs the engine side method and the
`endpoint_plugins` entry exposes it over HTTP. The two are registered and
loaded independently where neither implies the other.

Plugins are opt-in. See `load_endpoint_plugins` in
`vllm/plugins/__init__.py` for the loading/gating rules and
`docs/usage/security.md` for the security posture of exposing plugin defined
routes.

The CPU only render server (see `build_and_serve_renderer` in
`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/render`) has no `EngineClient`. A plugin
eligible for the `render` task (`required_tasks` is `None` or includes
`"render"`) still gets `attach_router` called but `init_state` receives
`engine_client=None`. Plugins that cannot function without an engine should
either exclude `"render"` from `required_tasks` or check for `None` in
`init_state`/their route handlers and degrade gracefully.

`EndpointPlugin`      *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.EndpointPlugin*

Bases: `Protocol`

Protocol implemented by `vllm.endpoint_plugins` entry point factories.

An entry point registered under the `vllm.endpoint_plugins` group must
resolve to a zero argument callable (a class or factory function) that
returns an object satisfying this protocol.

Methods: ~

- `attach_router` -- Register this plugin's routes on app.
- `init_state` -- Initialize per app state consumed by this plugin's routes.

Attributes: ~

- `name` (str) -- Unique plugin name used in logs and for VLLM_PLUGINS
  allowlisting.
- `required_tasks` (tuple[SupportedTask, ...] | None) -- Tasks the server
  must support for this plugin to be loaded.

                 *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.EndpointPlugin.name*
`name` `instance-attribute`

Unique plugin name used in logs and for `VLLM_PLUGINS` allowlisting.

       *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.EndpointPlugin.required_tasks*
`required_tasks` `instance-attribute`

Tasks the server must support for this plugin to be loaded.

The plugin is loaded only if this set intersects the server's
`supported_tasks`. `None` means the plugin has no task requirement and is
always eligible (subject to the `VLLM_PLUGINS` allowlist).

        *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.EndpointPlugin.attach_router*
`attach_router(app)`

Register this plugin's routes on `app`.

Called once during `build_app()` after all core routers have been attached.
HTTP routes registered here replace earlier routes with the same path
template and method. Other methods remain available.

           *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.EndpointPlugin.init_state*
`init_state(engine_client, state, args)` `async`

Initialize per app state consumed by this plugin's routes.

Called once during `init_app_state()` after core state has been initialized.
Use `engine_client` (e.g. `collective_rpc`) to reach the engine. Do not open
new engine access paths.

`engine_client` is `None` on the CPU only render server which has no engine.
This only happens for plugins eligible for the `render` task
(`required_tasks` is `None` or includes `"render"`). Handle `None`
explicitly (e.g. skip engine dependent setup, or have route handlers return
an error) if the plugin is loadable for `render` but cannot function without
an engine.

             *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.attach_endpoint_plugins*
`attach_endpoint_plugins(app, supported_tasks)`

Phase A of endpoint plugin wiring: discover, gate and attach routes.

Hooks run after all core routers have been attached. Plugin HTTP routes
replace earlier operations with the same path template and method in both
routing and OpenAPI. No-ops when no plugins are discovered/allowlisted.

         *vllm.plugins.endpoint_plugins.interface.init_endpoint_plugins_state*
`init_endpoint_plugins_state(engine_client, state, args)` `async`

Phase B of endpoint plugin wiring: initialize per app plugin state.

`state.endpoint_plugins` is set by `_attach_endpoint_plugins` (Phase A) in
`build_app`. Some `init_app_state` callers (e.g. `run_batch.py`) build their
own bare `State` without going through `build_app`. As a result
`endpoint_plugins` may be absent and are treated that the same as "none
attached".

`engine_client` is `None` for the CPU only render server which has no engine
(see `init_render_app_state`). Plugins must handle a `None` `engine_client`
themselves (see `EndpointPlugin.init_state`).

                                          *vllm.plugins.load_endpoint_plugins*
`load_endpoint_plugins(supported_tasks=None)`

Discover, gate and instantiate `vllm.endpoint_plugins` entry points.

Endpoint plugins add HTTP routes to the API server, so they default to not
loading. Unlike other plugin groups, a plugin here is only considered when
it is explicitly named in `VLLM_PLUGINS`. This is a stricter posture than
`load_plugins_by_group` which "load everything unless an allowlist says
otherwise". This posture is taken to handle potentially larger exposed
network surface.

  A discovered plugin is loaded only if both hold: ~

  - it is named in `VLLM_PLUGINS` (enforced by not calling the loader at all
    when `VLLM_PLUGINS` is unset). Note that `VLLM_PLUGINS=""` parses to
    `[""]`, not `None`, so it is treated as a (non strict) allowlist that
    matches no plugin name, not as "unset".
  - its `required_tasks` is `None` or intersects `supported_tasks`.

Parameters: ~

- `supported_tasks` (tuple[SupportedTask, ...] | None, default: None ) --
  Tasks the server supports. None means no plugin with a non None
  required_tasks will be loaded.

Returns: ~

- `list[EndpointPlugin]` -- Instantiated plugins that passed gating in
  discovery order.

`load_general_plugins()`                   *vllm.plugins.load_general_plugins*

WARNING: plugins can be loaded for multiple times in different processes.
They should be designed in a way that they can be loaded multiple times
without causing issues.

`load_plugins_by_group(group)`            *vllm.plugins.load_plugins_by_group*

Load plugins registered under the given entry point group.

`LateChunkingParams`                  *vllm.pooling_params.LateChunkingParams*

Bases: `Struct`

Fixed-length mean pooling before the token embedding head.

Requests recompute all prompt tokens, bypassing prefix cache reads. Special
tokens count toward chunk boundaries and are included in chunk means,
including the BOS token normally filtered from BGE-M3 token embeddings.

Attributes: ~

- `chunk_size` (int) -- Tokens per chunk, as an integer in [1, 2**63 - 1].

`LateInteractionParams`            *vllm.pooling_params.LateInteractionParams*

Bases: `Struct`

Metadata for worker-side late-interaction scoring.

Attributes: ~

- `mode` (`str`) --
  - "cache_query": cache query token embeddings
  - "score_doc": score a document against a cached query.

- `query_key` (str) -- stable key used for both DP routing and worker cache
  lookup.
- `query_uses` (int | None) -- expected number of document requests

`PoolingParams`                            *vllm.pooling_params.PoolingParams*

Bases: `Struct`

API parameters for pooling models.

Attributes: ~

  the pooler outputs. None uses the pooler's default, which is True in most
  cases.
- `dimensions` (int | None) -- Reduce the dimensions of embeddings if model
  support matryoshka representation.
- `late_chunking_params` (LateChunkingParams | None) -- Mean-pool contextual
  token states into fixed-size chunks for the token embedding task.

*vllm.reasoning.abs_reasoning_parsers.ReasoningParser.adjust_initial_state_from_prompt*
`adjust_initial_state_from_prompt(prompt_token_ids)`

Hook called once at the start of streaming with the prompt tokens.

Gives parsers a chance to adjust their initial parsing state based on the
prompt --- for example, when the chat template leaves the prompt inside an
open reasoning channel and the engine's default initial state would
otherwise misclassify the first generated tokens.

Default is a no-op; override in subclasses as needed.

         *vllm.reasoning.abs_reasoning_parsers.ReasoningParser.adjust_request*
`adjust_request(request)`

Adjust request parameters; override in subclasses as needed.

 *vllm.reasoning.abs_reasoning_parsers.ReasoningParser.count_reasoning_tokens*
`count_reasoning_tokens(token_ids)`

Count the number of reasoning tokens in a sequence.

Text-based reasoning models typically wrap their chain-of-thought between
special start/end tokens (e.g., `<think> ... </think>`). Implementations
that support reasoning token counting should override this method. The
default implementation returns `0` so existing parsers remain unchanged
unless they explicitly opt in.

Parameters: ~

- `token_ids` (Sequence[int]) -- Sequence of generated token ids (excluding
  prompt).

Returns: ~

- `int` ( int ) -- Number of tokens that belong to reasoning content.

*vllm.reasoning.abs_reasoning_parsers.ReasoningParser.has_engine_confirmed_reasoning_end*
`has_engine_confirmed_reasoning_end()`

Whether the engine has confirmed the reasoning end transition.

Engine-based parsers may defer terminal processing when the detokenizer
holds back text. This method returns the engine's processed state, not a raw
token-ID check.

Only called for parsers with `engine_based_streaming = True`.

`find_reasoning_end(token_ids)`

Find the first reasoning end in `token_ids`.

Returns its offset and whether its token is content, or
`ReasoningEnd(len(token_ids), False)` if there is none. Returns `None` if
the parser cannot locate reasoning ends by token id.

           *vllm.reasoning.ReasoningParser.has_engine_confirmed_reasoning_end*
`has_engine_confirmed_reasoning_end()`

Whether the engine has confirmed the reasoning end transition.

Engine-based parsers may defer terminal processing when the detokenizer
holds back text. This method returns the engine's processed state, not a raw
token-ID check.

Only called for parsers with `engine_based_streaming = True`.

                  *vllm.renderers.base.BaseRenderer._truncate_expanded_prompt*
`_truncate_expanded_prompt(engine_input, params)`

Re-apply `truncate_prompt_tokens` once placeholders are expanded.

`TokenizeParams.apply_post_tokenization` truncates the prompt before
multimodal expansion, so a single placeholder token can expand into many and
push the result back over the requested bound.

Multimodal spans are never cut: a request whose spans would not all survive
intact is rejected, matching the post-expansion rejection in
`vllm.v1.engine.input_processor._validate_model_input`.

Only multimodal inputs can grow after `apply_post_tokenization`, so
everything else returns immediately.

                       *vllm.renderers.base.BaseRenderer.clear_mm_cache_async*

`warmup(chat_params)`                *vllm.renderers.base.BaseRenderer.warmup*

Warm up this renderer to avoid first-request latency.

For chat requests: - Jinja2 template compilation

If a background multimodal warmup was launched (to overlap engine-core init)
it is joined first so it is not still touching the mm_processor_cache.
warmup_mm is idempotent, so the call below is a no-op if the background
warmup --- or a prior reset_mm_cache that joined it --- already ran it.

`_SwappableExecutor`                  *vllm.renderers.base._SwappableExecutor*

Bases: `Executor`

Executor whose inner pool can be replaced without changing identity.

`make_async` captures the executor object at wrap time. Replacing
`self._executor` with a new `ThreadPoolExecutor` would leave those wrappers
(tokenize, decode, pooling, derender) bound to a shutdown pool.

`max_input_tokens` `property` *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_input_tokens*

Maximum allowed number of input tokens.

`max_output_tokens` is not subtracted here: the value represents the actual
model context length, not a reservation of output space. Downstream clamping
of the sampling `max_tokens` is handled by `get_max_tokens()` in the
entrypoint layer.

                             *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_output_tokens*
`max_output_tokens = 0` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Maximum requested output tokens; `None` means no explicit limit.

Zero indicates a request that does not need generated tokens, such as
pooling.

                       *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_output_tokens_param*
`max_output_tokens_param = 'max_output_tokens'` `class-attribute`
`instance-attribute`

Override this to edit the message for validation errors.

                              *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_total_tokens*
`max_total_tokens` `instance-attribute`

Maximum allowed number of input + output tokens.

Usually, this refers to the model's context length.

                        *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_total_tokens_param*
`max_total_tokens_param = 'max_total_tokens'` `class-attribute`
`instance-attribute`

Override this to edit the message for validation errors.

                         *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.max_truncation_tokens*
`max_truncation_tokens` `property`

Maximum prompt length that truncation may reduce a prompt to.

For generative requests this is `max_input_tokens` less one, holding a token
of context back for output. Truncating to the full `max_total_tokens` would
leave `get_max_tokens()` clamping the sampling budget to 0, turning an
over-long prompt into a silent zero-token generation.

Pooling requests set `max_output_tokens = 0` and emit an embedding rather
than generated tokens, so they keep the full input budget.

                          *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.needs_detokenization*
`needs_detokenization = False` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Whether the tokenized prompt needs to contain the original text.

Not to be confused with `SamplingParams.detokenize` which deals with the
output generated by the model.

                             *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.pad_prompt_tokens*
`pad_prompt_tokens = None` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Number of tokens to pad to: - `None` means no padding. - `-1` maps to
`max_input_tokens`.

                          *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.return_token_offsets*
`return_token_offsets = False` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

                        *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.truncate_prompt_tokens*

                               *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams.truncation_side*

Which side to truncate from when `truncate_prompt_tokens` is active: -

the last N tokens (truncate from the start). - `None` falls back to the
tokenizer default.

                   *vllm.renderers.TokenizeParams._get_text_truncation_offset*

`_text_len_check` pre-truncates long text before tokenization when an
explicit truncation side is requested. Fast-tokenizer offsets are then
relative to that shortened string, so callers need this prefix length to map
them back to the original prompt.

                       *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.logprob_token_ids*
`logprob_token_ids = None` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Specific token IDs to return logprobs for. More efficient than logprobs=-1
when you only need logprobs for a small set of tokens. When set, logprobs
for exactly these token IDs will be returned, in addition to the sampled
token. This is useful for scoring tasks where you want to compare
probabilities of specific label tokens.

                                *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.logprobs*
`logprobs = None` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Number of log probabilities to return per output token. When set to `None`,
no probability is returned. If set to a non-`None` value, the result
includes the log probabilities of the specified number of most likely
tokens, as well as the chosen tokens. Note that the implementation follows
the OpenAI API: The API will always return the log probability of the
sampled token, so there may be up to `logprobs+1` elements in the response.
When set to -1, return all `vocab_size` log probabilities.

Maximum number of tokens to generate per output sequence.

`min_p = 0.0` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Represents the minimum probability for a token to be considered, relative to
the probability of the most likely token. Must be in [0, 1]. Set to 0 to
disable this.

                              *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.min_tokens*
`min_tokens = 0` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

                                       *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.n*
`n = 1` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Number of outputs to return for the given prompt request.

The maximum allowed value is controlled by the `VLLM_MAX_N_SEQUENCES`
environment variable (default: 16384).

  NOTE: ~

  `AsyncLLM` streams outputs by default. When `n > 1`, all `n` outputs are
  generated and streamed cumulatively per request. To see all `n` outputs
  upon completion, use `output_kind=RequestOutputKind.FINAL_ONLY` in
  `SamplingParams`.

`num_logprobs` `property`   *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.num_logprobs*

Number of sample logprobs to return per output token, or `None` if no sample
logprobs were requested. Takes `logprob_token_ids` into account: when
`logprobs` is unset but `logprob_token_ids` is set, returns
`len(logprob_token_ids)`.

                *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_token_ids*

                    *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.repetition_detection*
`repetition_detection = None` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Parameters for detecting repetitive N-gram patterns in output tokens. If
such repetition is detected, generation will be ended early. LLMs can
sometimes generate repetitive, unhelpful token patterns, stopping only when
they hit the maximum output length (e.g. 'abcdabcdabcd...' or '\emoji \emoji
\emoji ...'). This feature can detect such behavior and terminate early,
saving time and tokens.

                      *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.repetition_penalty*
`repetition_penalty = 1.0` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

Penalizes new tokens based on whether they appear in the prompt and the
generated text so far. Values > 1 encourage the model to use new tokens,
while values < 1 encourage the model to repeat tokens.

             *vllm.sampling_params.SamplingParams.routed_experts_prompt_start*
`routed_experts_prompt_start = 0` `class-attribute` `instance-attribute`

When enable_return_routed_experts is active, skip the first
routed_experts_prompt_start prompt tokens from the returned routing data. In
multi-turn agent scenarios, set this to the length of the already-returned
prefix to avoid duplicating routing for prompt tokens covered by earlier
turns. Default 0 returns routing for all prompt tokens.

- `ScalarType` -- ScalarType can represent a wide range of floating point
  and integer

`ScalarType` `dataclass`                         *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType*

ScalarType can represent a wide range of floating point and integer types,
in particular it can be used to represent sub-byte data types (something
that torch.dtype currently does not support). It is also capable of
representing types with a bias, i.e.: `stored_value = value + bias`, this is
useful for quantized types (e.g. standard GPTQ 4bit uses a bias of 8). The
implementation for this class can be found in csrc/core/scalar_type.hpp,
these type signatures should be kept in sync with that file.

Methods: ~

- `__str__` -- Naming generally follows: https://github.com/jax-ml/ml_dtypes
- `float_` -- Create a non-standard floating point type
- `float_IEEE754` -- Create a standard floating point type
- `has_bias` -- If the type has a non-zero bias.
- `has_infs` -- If the type is floating point and supports infinity.
- `int_` -- Create a signed integer scalar type (size_bits includes
  sign-bit).
- `is_floating_point` -- If the type is a floating point type.
- `is_ieee_754` -- If the type is a floating point type that follows IEEE
  754
- `is_integer` -- If the type is an integer type.
- `is_signed` -- If the type is signed (i.e. has a sign bit), same as signed
- `max` -- Max representable value for this scalar type.
- `min` -- Min representable value for this scalar type.
- `uint` -- Create an unsigned integer scalar type.

Attributes: ~

- `bias` (int) -- bias used to encode the values in this scalar type
- `exponent` (int) -- Number of bits in the exponent if this is a floating
  point type
- `id` (int) -- Convert the ScalarType to an int which can be passed to
  pytorch custom
- `mantissa` (int) -- Number of bits in the mantissa if this is a floating
  point type,
- `nan_repr` (NanRepr) -- How NaNs are represent in this scalar type,
  returns NanRepr value.
- `signed` (bool) -- If the type is signed (i.e. has a sign bit)

                             *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType._finite_values_only*

Private: if infs are supported, used `has_infs()` instead.

`bias` `instance-attribute`                 *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.bias*

bias used to encode the values in this scalar type (value = stored_value -
bias, default 0) for example if we store the type as an unsigned integer
with a bias of 128 then the value 0 will be stored as 128 and -1 will be
stored as 127 and 1 will be stored as 129.

`exponent` `instance-attribute`         *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.exponent*

Number of bits in the exponent if this is a floating point type (zero if
this an integer type)

`id` `cached` `property`                      *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.id*

This layout of the int must be kept in sync with the C++ ScalarType's
from_id method.

`mantissa` `instance-attribute`         *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.mantissa*

number bits representing an integer excluding the sign bit if this an
integer type.

If the type is signed (i.e. has a sign bit)

`__str__()`                              *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.__str__*

Naming generally follows: https://github.com/jax-ml/ml_dtypes for floating
point types (leading f) the scheme is:
`float<size_bits>_e<exponent_bits>m<mantissa_bits>[flags]` flags: -
no-flags: means it follows IEEE 754 conventions - f: means finite values
only (no infinities) - n: means nans are supported (non-standard encoding)
for integer types the scheme is: `[u]int<size_bits>[b<bias>]` - if bias is
not present it means its zero

                                          *vllm.scalar_type.ScalarType.float_*

conventions).

                                   *vllm.tokenizers.hf.maybe_make_thread_pool*
`maybe_make_thread_pool(tokenizer, copies=1)`

If `tokenizer` is a `TokenizersBackend`, modify the tokenizer in-place to
make the public interface thread-safe by routing calls through a deep-copied
tokenizer pool.

Note that: - Only `TokenizerLike`'s public interface is thread-safe. This
doesn't include `_tokenizer` property nor any mutation methods like
`add_special_tokens` or `add_tokens`. - Adjacent method calls could happen
on different deep copies.

                                                *vllm.triton_utils.allocation*

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher*

Registry for overriding Triton kernels with platform implementations.

Non-CUDA platforms can replace Triton kernels defined in vLLM core without
modifying core code:

>python
    from vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher import register_kernels

    register_kernels({
        "vllm.v1.worker.gpu.input_batch._prepare_pos_seq_lens_kernel": my_impl,
    })
<
The same call covers Triton device functions (`@triton.jit` helpers called
from inside other kernels and inlined at compile time): an implementation
that is itself a Triton kernel is swapped in directly, so outer kernels keep
compiling and launchable kernels run natively. Only non-Triton
implementations (plain callables, grid-remapping launchers) are wrapped in a
launch adapter.

Classes: ~

- `KernelOverride` -- Stand in for a Triton kernel, routing launches to a
  non-Triton impl.

Functions: ~

- `register_kernels` -- Register platform-specific implementations for
  Triton kernels.

`KernelOverride`                 *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher.KernelOverride*

Stand in for a Triton kernel, routing launches to a non-Triton `impl`.

Used by `register_kernels` for implementations that are not themselves
Triton kernels (plain callables, grid-remapping launchers); Triton kernel
implementations are swapped in directly and never wrapped.

The JIT warmup infrastructure launches kernels as `kernel[grid](**kwargs)`
where `kwargs` are keyed by the original kernel's argument names. This
wrapper forwards those launch arguments to the platform implementation: by
keyword when the implementation's parameter names match the kernel's,
otherwise positionally in the kernel's parameter order. An implementation
that reimplements the `kernel[grid]` protocol (a grid-remapping launcher)
receives the caller's grid. Compile-only JIT warmup
(`kernel.warmup(grid, **kwargs)`) is delegated to the implementation's own
`warmup` when present, and is a no-op otherwise.

Methods: ~

- `__getitem__` -- Bind a launch grid, mirroring Triton's kernel[grid].
- `warmup` -- Delegate compile-only warmup to the implementation.

`__getitem__(grid)`  *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher.KernelOverride.__getitem__*

Bind a launch grid, mirroring Triton's `kernel[grid]`.

A platform override that is itself a Triton kernel (or any object
implementing `__getitem__`) takes over the launch natively:
`impl[grid](*args, **kwargs)` binds against the override's own signature, so
the caller's grid reaches the override unchanged. Such an override must
mirror the original kernel's parameter names (or order), since launch sites
key arguments by the original names. Plain-callable overrides are invoked
with the launch arguments directly.

                          *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher.KernelOverride.warmup*
`warmup(grid=None, **kwargs)`

Delegate compile-only warmup to the implementation.

The JIT warmup machinery compiles warmup-owned kernels as
`kernel.warmup(grid, **kwargs)`. Forward that to the implementation's own
kernel so the override is what gets compiled. Implementations without a
warmable Triton kernel (plain callables, grid-remapping launchers) have
nothing to warm up and compile lazily on first launch.

`_is_triton_kernel(obj)`      *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher._is_triton_kernel*

Whether `obj` is a real Triton kernel (JITFunction).

Triton kernels (both launchable kernels and device functions called from
inside other kernels) expose the JIT launch protocol; plain callables and
grid-remapping launcher objects do not.

`_kernel_arg_names(kernel)`   *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher._kernel_arg_names*

Return the argument names of a Triton kernel or its fallback.

`_rebind_impls(replacements)`     *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher._rebind_impls*

Point every reference to each original object at its replacement.

A kernel or device-function object can be captured in two kinds of places
besides its defining module, and both must be patched for the overrides to
take effect everywhere:

- plain attributes of other modules (`from mod import kernel` copies),
  rebound to the replacement;
- JIT warmup owners, whose `kernel` attribute is the kernel they launch;
  swapped, and their cached `_kernel_arg_names` invalidated so the launch
  binding re-derives from the replacement.

One pass over `sys.modules` handles all objects in `replacements`.

`_resolve_kernel(name)`         *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher._resolve_kernel*

Return the (host object, attribute) holding the kernel `name`.

`register_kernels(overrides)`  *vllm.triton_utils.dispatcher.register_kernels*

Register platform-specific implementations for Triton kernels.

Parameters: ~

- `overrides`

  (`Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]]`) --

  Mapping from fully qualified kernel name to the platform implementation.
  Kernel names look like
  "vllm.v1.worker.gpu.input_batch._prepare_pos_seq_lens_kernel"; for kernels
  owned by a JIT warmup class, include the attribute path, e.g.
  "module.KernelClass.kernel".

  An implementation that is itself a Triton kernel (also the only kind that
  works for Triton device functions, which are inlined into other kernels at
  compile time) is swapped in directly and launches natively:
  `impl[grid](*args, **kwargs)` binds against the implementation's own
  signature and the caller's grid reaches it unchanged. Such an
  implementation must mirror the original kernel's parameter names (or
  order).

  Any other implementation (a plain callable, or a launcher that rewrites
  the grid for a non-CUDA device) is invoked with the launch arguments in
  the original kernel's parameter order (or by keyword when its parameter
  names match the kernel's).

`UsageMessage`                             *vllm.usage.usage_lib.UsageMessage*

Collect platform information and send it to the usage stats server.

                  *vllm.usage.usage_lib.UsageMessage._report_continuous_usage*
`_report_continuous_usage()`

Report usage every 10 minutes.

This helps us to collect more data points for uptime of vLLM usages. This
function can also help send over performance metrics over time.

`is_usage_stats_enabled()`       *vllm.usage.usage_lib.is_usage_stats_enabled*

Determine whether or not we can send usage stats to the server. The logic is
as follows: - By default, it should be enabled. - Three environment
variables can disable it: - VLLM_DO_NOT_TRACK=1 - DO_NOT_TRACK=1 -
VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1 - A file in the home directory can disable it if it
exists: - $HOME/.config/vllm/do_not_track

                                 *vllm.usage.usage_lib.set_runtime_usage_data*
`set_runtime_usage_data(key, value)`

Set global usage data that will be sent with every usage heartbeat.

     *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.FlexibleArgumentParser._pull_args_from_config*
`_pull_args_from_config(args)`

Method to pull arguments specified in the config file into the command-line
args variable.

The arguments in config file will be inserted between the argument list.

Example:

>yaml
        port: 12323
        tensor-parallel-size: 4
<
>python
    $: vllm {serve,chat,complete} "facebook/opt-12B" \
        --config config.yaml -tp 2
    $: args = [
        "serve,chat,complete",
        "facebook/opt-12B",
        '--config', 'config.yaml',
        '-tp', '2'
    ]
    $: args = [
        "serve,chat,complete",
        "facebook/opt-12B",
        '--port', '12323',
        '--tensor-parallel-size', '4',
        '-tp', '2'
        ]
<
Please note how the config args are inserted after the sub command. this way
the order of priorities is maintained when these are args parsed by super().

           *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.FlexibleArgumentParser.load_config_file*
`load_config_file(file_path)`

Loads a yaml file and returns the key value pairs as a flattened list with
argparse like pattern.

Supports both flat configs and nested YAML structures.

Flat config example:

>yaml
        port: 12323
        tensor-parallel-size: 4
<
returns: ['--port', '12323', '--tensor-parallel-size', '4']
Nested config example:

>yaml
        compilation-config:
          pass_config:
            fuse_allreduce_rms: true
        speculative-config:
          model: "nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v2"
          num_speculative_tokens: 3
<
returns: ['--compilation-config', '{"pass_config": {"fuse_allreduce_rms":
true}}', '--speculative-config', '{"model": "nvidia/gpt-oss-120b-Eagle3-v2",
...}']

`SortedHelpFormatter`          *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.SortedHelpFormatter*

Bases: `ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter`, `RawDescriptionHelpFormatter`

SortedHelpFormatter that sorts arguments by their option strings.

                  *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.SortedHelpFormatter._split_lines*
`_split_lines(text, width)`

1. Sentences split across lines have their single newlines removed.
2. Paragraphs and lists are split into separate lines.
3. Each line is wrapped to the specified width (width of terminal).

`human_readable_int(value)`     *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.human_readable_int*

Parse human-readable integers like '1k', '2M', etc. Including decimal values
with decimal multipliers.

Examples: - '1k' -> 1,000 - '1K' -> 1,024 - '25.6k' -> 25,600

                        *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.human_readable_int_or_auto*
`human_readable_int_or_auto(value)`

Parse human-readable integers like '1k', '2M', etc. Including decimal values
with decimal multipliers. Also accepts -1 or 'auto' as a special value for
auto-detection.

Examples: - '1k' -> 1,000 - '1K' -> 1,024 - '25.6k' -> 25,600 - '-1' or
'auto' -> -1 (special value for auto-detection)

`summary_line(description)`           *vllm.utils.argparse_utils.summary_line*

                                                      *vllm.utils.async_utils*

Contains helpers related to asynchronous code.

This is similar in concept to the `asyncio` module.

Functions: ~

- `collect_from_async_generator` -- Collect all items from an async
  generator into a list.
- `make_async` -- Take a blocking function, and run it on in an executor
  thread.
- `make_async_with_semaphore` -- Take a blocking function, and run it on in
  an executor thread.
- `merge_async_iterators` -- Merge multiple asynchronous iterators into a
  single iterator.

                         *vllm.utils.async_utils.collect_from_async_generator*
`collect_from_async_generator(iterator)` `async`

Collect all items from an async generator into a list.

`make_async(func, executor=None)`          *vllm.utils.async_utils.make_async*

Take a blocking function, and run it on in an executor thread.

This function prevents the blocking function from blocking the asyncio event
loop. The code in this function needs to be thread safe.

                            *vllm.utils.async_utils.make_async_with_semaphore*
`make_async_with_semaphore(func, executor)`

Take a blocking function, and run it on in an executor thread.

This function prevents the blocking function from blocking the asyncio event
loop. The code in this function needs to be thread safe.

The function is wrapped in a semaphore to limit the number of concurrent
executions making it easier to cancel tasks before they start.

                                *vllm.utils.async_utils.merge_async_iterators*
`merge_async_iterators(*iterators)` `async`

Merge multiple asynchronous iterators into a single iterator.

This method handle the case where some iterators finish before others. When
it yields, it yields a tuple (i, item) where i is the index of the iterator
that yields the item.

`put_if_fits(key, value)`              *vllm.utils.cache.LRUCache.put_if_fits*

Insert `value` if it is not larger than the cache capacity.

Unlike `put`, this does not raise when a single item exceeds `maxsize`. Size
is computed once inside the insert path.

Returns: ~

- `bool` -- True if the item was cached, otherwise False.

`stat(*, delta=False)`                        *vllm.utils.cache.LRUCache.stat*

Gets the cumulative number of hits and queries against this cache.

If `delta=True`, instead gets these statistics since the last call that also
passed `delta=True`.
